newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bavaria deports more Bosnians despite criticism.
newsitem.headline: Bavaria deports more Bosnians despite criticism.

text.p: The southern German state of Bavaria said on Friday about 20 Bosnians have been deported in the last few days and it has now expelled 93 since it began repatriating war refugees.

Airport authorities in the conservative state, which has ignored criticism from inside and outside Germany, said most of those deported, often against their will, were young and single men and women. About a third were convicted criminals.

A social services agency at Munich's airport said that a large number of those deported had had jobs in Germany and several were detained on their way to work. Many were detained in jails for two or three days before being put on aircraft bound for Bosnia.
Last week several leading German public figures, including former foreign minister Hans-Dietrich Genscher, made a public appeal for changes to the practice of forcibly repatriating Bosnian refugees.

The signatories of the appeal, addressed to Interior Minister Manfred Kanther and his regional state counterparts, said the current practice could lead to increased tension in Bosnia and was damaging Germany's international image.

"As soon as peace bceomes reality in Bosnia, tens of thousands of Bosnians will return home voluntarily," the appeal said. "Those who know the situation also know that the state of peace has not yet been achieved in Bosnia."

The text was also signed by Ignatz Bubis, the leader of Germany's Jewish community, Bosnia mediator Christian Schwarz-Schilling and Hans Koschnick, the former European Union administrator of the Bosnian city of Mostar.
They singled out the deportation earlier this week of a group of Bosnian refugees from Berlin and Bavaria for criticism.
"Among those deported were pregnant women, patients receiving treatment for heart illness and other people whose deportation is incomprehensible," the signatories said.
They also said Germany was deporting refugees back to the Bosnian Serb entity, Republika Srpska, which they described as being "controlled by radical forces".

Germany took in more than 300,000 Bosnian refugees -- more than the rest of the European Union put together. Kanther and regional interior ministers agreed last year the refugees could be forcibly reptatriated if they refused to go home.
Conservative-ruled regional states have already carried out the practice but others have not resorted to it so far.
